# nish/net/fetch

An HTTP/1.1 client. `fetchSync(request, options)` is the blocking one for command-line programs: it dials, sends, and answers the response's head with a reader for its body, and a `FetchSyncClient` does the same while keeping one connection alive between fetches. `await fetch(url, init)` is the async one: it parks its task on `nish:async` instead of the thread, so `awaitAll(fetch(a), fetch(b))` overlaps the two.

```ts
import {
  FetchError,
  FetchPool,
  FetchResponse,
  FetchSyncClient,
  HTTP_E_BLOCKED,
  HTTP_E_BODY_TOO_LARGE,
  HTTP_E_CERTIFICATE,
  HTTP_E_CONNECT_TIMEOUT,
  HTTP_E_DNS,
  HTTP_E_IO,
  HTTP_E_NONE,
  HTTP_E_PROTOCOL,
  HTTP_E_PROXY,
  HTTP_E_PROXY_REFUSED,
  HTTP_E_READ_TIMEOUT,
  HTTP_E_REDIRECT_REFUSED,
  HTTP_E_REFUSED,
  HTTP_E_REQUEST,
  HTTP_E_TLS,
  HTTP_E_TOO_MANY_REDIRECTS,
  HTTP_E_TOTAL_TIMEOUT,
  HTTP_E_URL,
  HttpBodyReader,
  HttpOptions,
  HttpRequest,
  HttpResponse,
  RequestInit,
  fetch,
  fetchSync,
  httpChooseProxy,
  httpErrorName,
  httpNoProxyMatch,
  httpProxyFor,
} from "nish/net/fetch";
```

<scalar-code-group>

```ts example.ts
import { fetch } from "nish/net/fetch";

const r = await fetch("http://127.0.0.1:8080/health");
if (r.isOk()) {
  const body: string = r.value.text();
}
```

</scalar-code-group>

<scalar-callout type="info">

**The async `fetch`** answers a `Result`: a `FetchResponse` whose body was
read whole before it answered (up to `maxBodyBytes`, 256 MiB by default,
else `HTTP_E_BODY_TOO_LARGE`), or a `FetchError` with the `HTTP_E_*` code.
The connect, every write and every read wait on the executor; the name
lookup still blocks, and only `http://` is driven (an `https://` URL answers
`HTTP_E_TLS` naming `fetchSync`, never a silent block). A `FetchPool` handed
in through `RequestInit.pool` keeps idle connections per route, capped.
Policy, proxies, redirects and error codes are the shared code below, so
both clients behave alike. It does not run under `--emit-ts`.

</scalar-callout>

<scalar-code-group>

```ts example.ts
import { HttpOptions, HttpRequest, HttpResponse, fetchSync } from "nish/net/fetch";

const req = new HttpRequest("GET", "http://example.com/");
req.header("Accept", "application/json");
const res: HttpResponse | null = fetchSync(req, new HttpOptions());
if (res !== null) {
  const body: u8[] | null = res.body.readAll(1048576);
}
```

</scalar-code-group>

<scalar-detail title="It blocks the thread">

**It blocks the thread** at every step, the way a CLI wants it to: the
lookup, the connect, each write and each read. A server, which must not
stall every connection for one slow peer, drives `nish/net/http1-client-codec`'s
parser from its own loop instead. Every wait is bounded: `connectTimeoutMs`
for the lookup and the connect (one budget across every address the name
has), `readTimeoutMs` for each wait on the peer, and `totalTimeoutMs`, when
set, for the whole fetch, redirects and body included, so a server that
drips one byte a second cannot hold a fetch forever.

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-detail title="Framing is the parser's">

The head is written by `http1RequestHead` and
every byte read goes through `Http1ResponseParser`, so a value holding a CR
or LF is refused rather than sent, and every response-smuggling shape is
refused with the parser's own code (see `docs/security/http1-client-codec.md`).

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-detail title="Keep-alive">

**Keep-alive** holds one connection, to the last origin (or proxy) used. A
fetch to the same place reuses it once the last body has been read to its
end; a fetch while a body is unread closes it, and the old reader answers an
error. A reused connection the server closed while it sat idle is the one
failure a client cannot avoid, so a request with an idempotent method that
fails on it before any response byte arrives is sent once more on a fresh
connection (RFC 9110 §9.2.2). A POST is never sent twice.

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-detail title="Redirects">

**Redirects** are not followed unless `followRedirects` is set, and then
only to the same origin unless `crossOriginRedirects` is set too. A hop to
another origin drops `Authorization`, `Proxy-Authorization`, `Cookie` and
the caller's `Host`; a hop from https to http is always refused; 303 turns
any method but HEAD into a GET without a body, as do 301 and 302 after a
POST, and 307 and 308 keep the method and the body (RFC 9110 §15.4). Past
`maxRedirects` hops the fetch fails.

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-detail title="Proxies">

**Proxies** come from the environment when `useEnvProxy` is set:
`http_proxy` (or `HTTP_PROXY`), `https_proxy` (or `HTTPS_PROXY`) and
`no_proxy` (or `NO_PROXY`), the lower-case name first. `HTTP_PROXY` is
ignored when `REQUEST_METHOD` is set, since a CGI program finds a request's
`Proxy:` header there under that name (the "httpoxy" hole). Only an
`http://` proxy is accepted. An http request goes to it in absolute form; an
https one goes through a `CONNECT` tunnel.

</scalar-detail>

Every failure answers null with a distinct `HTTP_E_*` code in the client's
`error` and a sentence in `errorText`; a body reader answers the code
negated.

Private helpers share the importing program's flat symbol namespace
(`docs/wp26-stdlib.md` §3e), which is why each one carries the module's name.

Written from RFC 9110 and RFC 9112, not ported from another implementation.

## Functions

### fetch

Fetches `url` without blocking the process: the task waits on the
executor while the connection is made, the request written and the
response read, so other tasks run meanwhile and `awaitAll(fetch(a),
fetch(b))` overlaps the two. The body is read whole, up to
`maxBodyBytes`, before the answer comes. Only http is driven this way: an
https URL answers `HTTP_E_TLS` (use `fetchSync`). The name lookup still
blocks. Policy, proxy, redirect and error rules are `fetchSync`'s.

```ts
function fetch(
  url: string,
  init: RequestInit | null = null,
): Promise<Result<FetchResponse, FetchError>>
```

<scalar-field name="url" type="string" required>

The absolute `http://` URL to fetch.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="init" type="RequestInit | null">

The method, fields, body, options and pool; null for a plain `GET`.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="returns" type="Promise&lt;Result&lt;FetchResponse, FetchError&gt;&gt;">

The response with its body, or the failure: never a panic.

</scalar-field>

### fetchSync

One fetch on a client of its own, closed once the body has been read or
the fetch failed. Null on a failure, with no way to say why: a program
that reports its errors fetches through a `FetchSyncClient`.

```ts
function fetchSync(
  req: HttpRequest,
  options: HttpOptions,
): HttpResponse | null
```

<scalar-field name="req" type="HttpRequest" required>

The request to send, as a `FetchSyncClient` takes it.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="options" type="HttpOptions" required>

The client's limits, timeouts, TLS trust and proxies for this one fetch.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="returns" type="HttpResponse | null">

The response, the last one when redirects were followed, or null on any failure.

</scalar-field>

### httpChooseProxy

A proxy variable's value: `lower` when it is set and not empty, else
`upper` when `upperAllowed`, else "". `HTTP_PROXY` is not allowed under CGI.

```ts
function httpChooseProxy(
  lower: string | null,
  upper: string | null,
  upperAllowed: boolean,
): string
```

<scalar-field name="lower" type="string | null" required>

The lower-case variable's value, such as `http_proxy`'s, or null when it is unset.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="upper" type="string | null" required>

The upper-case variable's value, such as `HTTP_PROXY`'s, or null when it is unset.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="upperAllowed" type="boolean" required>

Whether the upper-case variable may be read: false for `HTTP_PROXY` under CGI, where a request's `Proxy` header sets it.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="returns" type="string">

The chosen variable's value, a proxy URL or for `no_proxy` a comma-separated host list, or "" when neither applies.

</scalar-field>

### httpErrorName

A short name for an `HTTP_E_*` code, for messages: "dns", "read timeout",
... A fetch's `errorText` starts with it.

```ts
function httpErrorName(code: i32): string
```

<scalar-field name="code" type="i32" required>

An `HTTP_E_*` code, such as a client's `error`.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="returns" type="string">

The code's name, "none" for `HTTP_E_NONE`, or "unknown" for a number that is no code.

</scalar-field>

### httpNoProxyMatch

Whether `noProxy`, a comma-separated list, names `host` on `port`: an entry
is `*` (every host), a name that matches the host or any domain under it
(with or without a leading dot), or an IP address that matches only itself;
any of them may end in `:port`, and an IPv6 address with a port is written
in brackets. Case does not matter. Address ranges are not understood.

```ts
function httpNoProxyMatch(
  noProxy: string,
  host: string,
  port: i32,
): boolean
```

<scalar-field name="noProxy" type="string" required>

The list, as `NO_PROXY` holds it; an entry that does not parse is skipped.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="host" type="string" required>

The request's host name or IP address; trailing dots do not matter.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="port" type="i32" required>

The port the request goes to.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="returns" type="boolean">

True when an entry names the host (and its port, if it has one), so the request goes direct.

</scalar-field>

### httpProxyFor

The proxy a request to `scheme://host:port` goes through, given the three
settings: `httpsProxy` for https, `httpProxy` for http, and "" for none or
when `noProxy` names the host.

```ts
function httpProxyFor(
  scheme: string,
  host: string,
  port: i32,
  httpProxy: string,
  httpsProxy: string,
  noProxy: string,
): string
```

<scalar-field name="scheme" type="string" required>

The request URL's scheme, lower-cased; one other than `http` or `https` gets no proxy.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="host" type="string" required>

The request URL's host, matched against `noProxy`.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="port" type="i32" required>

The port the request goes to, matched against an entry's `:port`.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="httpProxy" type="string" required>

The proxy URL for `http` requests, or "" for none.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="httpsProxy" type="string" required>

The proxy URL for `https` requests, or "" for none.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="noProxy" type="string" required>

The comma-separated hosts that go direct, as `httpNoProxyMatch` reads them.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="returns" type="string">

The proxy URL the request goes through, or "" when it goes direct.

</scalar-field>

## Classes

### FetchError

Why an async `fetch` failed: an `HTTP_E_*` code and its sentence, the
code's name first, as `FetchSyncClient.errorText` reads. The text never
holds a URL's credentials or query.

```ts
class FetchError
```

| Member | |
| --- | --- |
| `new FetchError(code: i32, text: string)` | A failure with its code and text. |
| `code: i32` | The `HTTP_E_*` code. |
| `text: string` | The code's name, a colon and what went wrong, such as `dns: example.invalid could not be looked up`. |

### FetchPool

Connections an async `fetch` leaves open for the next one to the same
place, held by the caller and handed in through `RequestInit.pool`. At
most `maxIdlePerOrigin` wait per route and 64 in all; a kept connection
the server closed, or sent a byte on unasked, is closed when it is next
looked at. A fetch under an outbound policy never keeps or takes one.

```ts
class FetchPool
```

| Member | |
| --- | --- |
| `new FetchPool(maxIdlePerOrigin: i32 = 4)` | An empty pool. |
| `maxIdlePerOrigin: i32` | The most idle connections kept for one route (origin, or proxy). |
| `close(): void` | Closes every idle connection; the pool can still keep new ones. |
| `idle(): i32` | How many idle connections the pool holds. |

### FetchResponse

A response `fetch` answered, its body already read whole: the body is
read before `fetch` answers, up to `maxBodyBytes`, so `text()` and
`bytes()` are plain calls. `names` are lower-cased and in the order they
arrived, beside `values`; `url` is the URL that answered.

```ts
class FetchResponse
```

| Member | |
| --- | --- |
| `new FetchResponse()` | A response with no status, fields or body yet; `fetch` fills them in. |
| `body: u8[]` | The body, de-chunked; empty for a `HEAD` or a status that has none. |
| `names: string[]` | The header field names, lower-cased, in the order they arrived. |
| `reason: string` | The reason phrase the server sent beside the status. |
| `status: i32` | The status code, such as 200. |
| `url: string` | The URL that answered, which differs from the request's after a redirect. |
| `values: string[]` | The header field values, each beside its name in `names`. |
| `bytes(): u8[]` | The body's bytes. |
| `header(name: string): string \| null` | The first value of the field `name`, in any case. |
| `text(): string` | The body as a string, its bytes unchanged: nothing checks that they are UTF-8. |

### FetchSyncClient

A client: the options, the proxy settings, and at most one open
connection, kept between fetches. Not for two threads at once.

```ts
class FetchSyncClient
```

| Member | |
| --- | --- |
| `new FetchSyncClient(options: HttpOptions)` | A client with no connection open yet, its proxy settings read from the environment when `useEnvProxy` is set. |
| `error: i32` | The last failure's `HTTP_E_*` code; `HTTP_E_NONE` after a fetch that answered. |
| `errorText: string` | A sentence saying why the last failure happened, for a log; "" after a fetch that answered. |
| `options: HttpOptions` | The options every fetch through this client follows. |
| `reused: boolean` | Whether `fd` has carried a response before the one in flight. |
| `close(): void` | Closes the connection; the client can still fetch, on a new one. |
| `fetch(req: HttpRequest): HttpResponse \| null` | Sends `req` and answers the response once its head is in, following redirects as the options say; null on a failure, with `error` and `errorText` set. The body is read through the response's `body` before the next fetch. |
| `setProxies(httpProxy: string, httpsProxy: string, noProxy: string): void` | Replaces the proxy settings, as the three variables would set them; "" for none. |

### HttpBodyReader

A response's body, read as it arrives: de-chunked, bounded by
`maxBodyBytes`, and ending where the framing says it ends, so a cut-short
body is an error and never taken for a whole one. It reads through the
client that made it, and only until that client starts its next fetch.

```ts
class HttpBodyReader
```

| Member | |
| --- | --- |
| `new HttpBodyReader(client: FetchSyncClient, generation: i32)` | A reader for the body of one response. |
| `client: FetchSyncClient` | The client that made the response; it carries the connection the body arrives on. |
| `read(buf: u8[], off: i32, n: i32): i32` | Up to `n` body bytes into `buf[off ..]`: how many (at least one), 0 at the end of the body, or a negated `HTTP_E_*` code, the client's `errorText` saying why. It waits for at least one byte, no more, so an event stream is read event by event. A window outside `buf` panics; an empty one answers 0 at once, reading nothing, so 0 means the end only when `n` is positive. |
| `readAll(limit: i32): u8[] \| null` | The rest of the body in one array, or null on an error or once it passes `limit` bytes (`HTTP_E_BODY_TOO_LARGE`, and the connection is closed). |

### HttpOptions

How a client behaves. Every field has a default meant for a CLI talking to
an API; raise `maxBodyBytes` to download something large, and set
`readTimeoutMs` to 0 for an event stream that may be quiet for a long time.

```ts
class HttpOptions
```

| Member | |
| --- | --- |
| `new HttpOptions()` |  |
| `connectTimeoutMs: i32` | The budget for the lookup and the connect together; 0 or less for none but the total. |
| `crossOriginRedirects: boolean` | Let a followed redirect go to another origin (see the module comment). |
| `followRedirects: boolean` | Follow a redirect rather than answer it; only to the same origin unless `crossOriginRedirects` is set. |
| `maxBodyBytes: i64` | 256 MiB by default; a body past it fails with `HTTP_E_BODY_TOO_LARGE`. |
| `maxHeaderBytes: i32` | The status line and the header section, each at most this. |
| `maxRedirects: i32` | The most redirect hops one fetch follows; past them the fetch fails. |
| `outbound: OutboundPolicy \| null` | For a URL the program did not choose: only the addresses and hosts the policy allows are reached, no proxy is used, and its caps apply (see `nish/net/outbound`). Null for none. |
| `readTimeoutMs: i32` | The longest wait for the server to send or take a byte; 0 or less for none. |
| `rootsPemPath: string \| null` | A PEM file of the roots an https server's chain must end at; null for the system's. |
| `totalTimeoutMs: i32` | The budget for a whole fetch, its body included; 0 or less for none. |
| `useEnvProxy: boolean` | Read the proxy settings from the environment (see the module comment). |

### HttpRequest

One request: a method, an absolute `http://` or `https://` URL, header
fields in the order they are sent, and an optional body. A `Host` field is
added from the URL unless the caller gives one, and `Content-Length` from
the body, so a caller never frames the body itself. Userinfo in the URL is
not sent anywhere: a program that means to authenticate sets its own
`Authorization` field, so a password is never sent by accident.

```ts
class HttpRequest
```

| Member | |
| --- | --- |
| `new HttpRequest(method: string, url: string)` | A request with no header fields and no body. |
| `body: u8[] \| null` | Null for no body at all; an empty array sends `Content-Length: 0`. |
| `method: string` | The request method, sent as given, such as `GET` or `POST`. |
| `names: string[]` | The header field names, in the order they are sent. |
| `url: string` | The absolute URL the request is sent to. |
| `values: string[]` | The header field values, each beside its name in `names`. |
| `header(name: string, value: string): void` | Appends one header field; nothing is checked until the request is written. |

### HttpResponse

A response's head, as the server sent it, and a reader for its body. `url`
is the URL that answered, which differs from the request's after a redirect.
`names` are lower-cased and in the order they arrived, beside `values`.

```ts
class HttpResponse
```

| Member | |
| --- | --- |
| `new HttpResponse(body: HttpBodyReader)` | A response with no status and no fields yet; the client fills them in. |
| `body: HttpBodyReader` | The reader for the response's body. |
| `names: string[]` | The header field names, lower-cased, in the order they arrived. |
| `reason: string` | The reason phrase the server sent beside the status. |
| `status: i32` | The status code, such as 200. |
| `url: string` | The URL that answered, which differs from the request's after a redirect. |
| `values: string[]` | The header field values, each beside its name in `names`. |
| `header(name: string): string \| null` | The first value of the field `name`, in any case. |

### RequestInit

What an async `fetch` sends and how it behaves. `options` are
`HttpOptions` as `fetchSync` reads them, except that `readTimeoutMs`
bounds no wait (a wait has no deadline yet), `connectTimeoutMs` bounds
only the name lookup, and `totalTimeoutMs` is checked each time a wait
ends. `pool` keeps connections for later fetches; null closes each one
when its fetch is done.

```ts
class RequestInit
```

| Member | |
| --- | --- |
| `new RequestInit()` | A `GET` with no fields, no body, default options and no pool. |
| `body: u8[] \| null` | Null for no body at all; an empty array sends `Content-Length: 0`. |
| `method: string` | The request method, sent as given; `GET` by default. |
| `names: string[]` | The header field names, in the order they are sent. |
| `options: HttpOptions` | The limits, policy and redirect and proxy settings (see above for the timeouts). |
| `pool: FetchPool \| null` | Where idle connections are kept between fetches; null for none. |
| `values: string[]` | The header field values, each beside its name in `names`. |
| `header(name: string, value: string): RequestInit` | Appends one header field; nothing is checked until the request is written. |

<scalar-card title="11" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`HTTP_E_PROXY_REFUSED: i32`

The proxy answered its CONNECT with something other than 2xx.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="5" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`HTTP_E_READ_TIMEOUT: i32`

The server sent nothing, or took nothing, for `readTimeoutMs`.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="9" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`HTTP_E_REDIRECT_REFUSED: i32`

A redirect to another origin, from https to http, or to a URL that is not http or https.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="3" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`HTTP_E_REFUSED: i32`

Every address of the host refused the connection, or could not be reached.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="14" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`HTTP_E_REQUEST: i32`

The request itself was refused before a byte was sent: a bad method, header or target.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="12" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`HTTP_E_TLS: i32`

The TLS handshake or a TLS record failed.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="8" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`HTTP_E_TOO_MANY_REDIRECTS: i32`

A redirect past `maxRedirects`.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="6" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`HTTP_E_TOTAL_TIMEOUT: i32`

The fetch ran past `totalTimeoutMs`.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="1" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`HTTP_E_URL: i32`

The request's URL is not an absolute http or https URL.

</scalar-card>

</scalar-grid>
